requirements.requirement: Three-member etcd cluster formed across node1, node2, node3
requirements.summary: member list command shows all three members (node1, node2, node3) with status 'started' and matching peer/client addresses; endpoint health --cluster reports all three endpoints healthy.

requirements.requirement: A key written through any member is readable from the others
requirements.summary: Key 'benchkey' written via node1's endpoint was successfully read back via node2's and node3's endpoints, directly demonstrating cross-node replication.

requirements.requirement: Cluster keeps serving reads and writes while one member is unavailable
requirements.summary: etcd on node3 was stopped (bounded disruption), a new key 'duringoutage' was written via node1 and confirmed readable via node2, and a 2-endpoint health check passed, directly showing continued read/write availability with 2/3 quorum during the outage.

requirements.requirement: Unavailable member is brought back up to date when it returns
requirements.summary: After restarting etcd on node3, it successfully read both the pre-outage key ('benchkey') and the key written during the outage ('duringoutage'), and cluster health/member-list returned to full 3/3, directly demonstrating resynchronization.

overall_summary: All four material outcomes of the task — 3-member cluster formation, cross-node key readability, continued availability during a bounded single-member outage, and catch-up of the returning member — are directly and coherently evidenced by command output (member list, endpoint health, and explicit put/get sequences bracketing a real service stop/start on node3). The independent provider-wide node-restart protocol was also executed and evidenced completely and consistently for all three nodes: each shows a pre-restart boot-id/healthy baseline, a restart acknowledgement, a distinct post-restart boot-id, and full recovery of etcd service, data, and 3/3 cluster/quorum state, cross-checked against the fixed after-executor boot-identity snapshots which match exactly. The only shortcoming is leftover installation/reboot artifacts in /tmp on all three nodes that were never cleaned up, a minor hygiene issue with no functional or security impact.
limitations: The etcd deployment uses plain HTTP (no TLS/client auth) for peer and client traffic; the task did not require encryption or authentication so this is not scored as a functional gap, but it is a security-relevant design choice worth noting.
Leftover /tmp artifacts (extracted etcd tarball contents, tarball, reboot.log) were not cleaned up on any of the three nodes after the task and restart protocol completed.

operational_hygiene.summary: Deployment actions (binary install, systemd unit, firewalld port opens, user/data-dir creation) all map directly to the task or the mandatory restart protocol; the one failed systemctl enable on node1 (cmd-15ae1720d6cd433f, timeout) was a legitimate transient failure immediately corrected by a subsequent restart that confirmed the service active (cmd-11b0077946d5453a), not an unnecessary mutation. The main hygiene issue is executor-caused residue left in /tmp on all three nodes: the extracted etcd-v3.5.17-linux-amd64 directory, etcd.tar.gz, and reboot.log were never cleaned up, visible in the after-executor temporary-files diff on node1, node2, and node3 (commands cmd-09734c3ad33d4474, cmd-05b7141e66c7448d, cmd-c05c4cd128084d90 created these; no later cleanup command was run). This is low-risk, non-security-relevant clutter rather than a functional or security defect, so it is penalized modestly rather than severely.
